title: From Cart to Confirmation: Checkout Orchestration
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/11-cart-and-checkout/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: where the published chapter did not do what the spec asks, the gap is listed under open_questions and the prose was revised to match.

know: The difference between a cart (a draft that reserves and promises nothing), checkout (a clocked sequence that asks for final answers) and the order (the record the rest of the platform must keep).
What checkout calls, in what order, and how fresh each answer must be.
The four ways to run a checkout, and the mechanisms through which platforms let merchants change it.
believe: Checkout should own none of the facts it writes into the order.
The payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, decides that a payment succeeded.
can_do: Draw their own checkout's call sequence and say which answers come from copies.
Judge a proposal to customize checkout by its mechanism and by the vendor's support date for that mechanism.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who has just inherited a checkout (Noor Visser's position). The e-commerce manager who asks for checkout changes and the finance lead who sees unpaid orders at month-end are the secondary readers.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Kestrel & Pine, its people (Noor Visser, Milan Petrov, Daniel Okafor, Sanne de Wit), its 2026 incidents in outline and the names of the failure patterns (meet-kestrel-and-pine, where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), what a 'system' is, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Part II: one written price rule with prices selected once at order placement and frozen; promotions as data with an evaluation order; available-to-promise with one writer each for on hand and committed and an exact commit at checkout; the Black Friday Oversell, where the platform's stock copy was up to two hours old.

From the Part III introduction: one order passes through four owners (checkout, the payment provider, the order record, the ledger), and Eva's order #1072455 is created at 21:14 on 13 April 2027 with its payment pending.
does_not_know: Cart, checkout and order as three different things; orchestration; reserve-on-add.
Freshness of an answer at the moment of commitment; the payment session and its expiry.
The detour to the bank's app, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication, the idempotency key on order creation, the payment outcome as external truth.
Guest checkout, express wallet and payment token; conversion and abandoned cart.
Company account, contract price list, reverse charge, payment terms, credit check.
Hosted checkout, extension point, time budget, headless checkout, PCI DSS and its self-assessment questionnaire, sandboxed function.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a shopper who pays in her bank's app and never returns, and a payment notification delivered twice, the reader says when the order is created, what marks it paid and why the repeat changes nothing.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A shopper pays by iDEAL in her bank's app and never returns to the shop; the payment provider's notification then arrives twice. Using only this chapter: when should the order have been created, what marks it paid, and what does the second notification do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The order is created at confirmation with the payment pending, keyed on the cart and the payment (an idempotency key), not on the thank-you page; the provider's signed webhook moves it to paid; the second webhook changes nothing because its event is recognized as already applied; a daily job asks the provider about orders still pending after the method's expiry window.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a checkout that kept selling a product the warehouse no longer had, the reader places the fault in the system that answered the availability call, not in checkout.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On a peak evening the checkout kept selling a jacket for up to two hours after the warehouse ran out. Using only this chapter: where was the fault, and is the fix in the checkout?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Checkout trusted the availability answer it was given, which came from the platform's copy of stock refreshed up to two hours earlier; checkout owns no stock figure. The fix is in who answers the availability call at order creation (a current answer from an availability service, W1), not in checkout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an agency's proposal to inject a script into the checkout, the reader names the sanctioned alternative and the two risks of the script.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An agency proposes to add a gift-wrap option by injecting a script into the checkout's payment page. Using only this chapter: what should the merchant do instead, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Use a sanctioned extension point of the platform, which runs with a time limit and is versioned. A third-party script on the payment page falls under the card industry's script rules (PCI DSS) and can read every card number typed there, and a mechanism outside the sanctioned ones is withdrawn on a date the vendor announces (Shopify's checkout.liquid and Scripts); keep an inventory of each customization, its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a price, the last unit or the payment answer can change while the shopper checks out; what checkout must call and how it creates one order despite retries; Eva's checkout as the worked example; four ways to run checkout; Shopify's 2023–2026 changes as the case for limits on customization. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's checkout, vendor documentation, Shopify's dated changelog.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What happens between "add to cart" and "order confirmed", and why do platforms restrict what merchants may change in checkout?
thesis.claim: Between 'add to cart' and 'order confirmed', checkout asks each system that owns a fact for a final answer (price, tax, availability, delivery promise, payment), writes those answers into the order and creates the order exactly once, keyed on the cart and the payment rather than on a page load, leaving the payment provider's signed message, not the thank-you page, to mark it paid. Platforms restrict merchant changes to named extension points with time limits because every order passes through checkout: merchant code there can delay or fail order creation at peak, a script on the payment page can read the card numbers typed into it, and a template the merchant edits cannot follow the platform's upgrades.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that checkout is the storefront's last few pages, which a merchant or its agency may edit like any other page, and that the order exists, paid, once the shopper reaches the thank-you page.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's checkout kept selling the Ridgewalker jacket for up to two hours after Duiven ran out on Black Friday 2026 because checkout wrote the answer of an out-of-date stock copy into each order and the warehouse could not keep those orders; the fix is to have a current availability service answer that call, not to change checkout. A merchant that accepts the claim lists what its checkout calls and which answers come from copies, creates orders keyed on the cart and the payment and settles them by webhook and a daily job, and customizes checkout only through sanctioned extension points listed with the vendor's support date; Shopify withdrew editable checkout templates and scripts on dated deadlines between August 2024 and August 2026.
thesis.how_why: The warehouse, finance and the customer all act on what checkout writes into the order, so a stale price or stock figure written there becomes their error. The shopper leaves for her bank's app or a 3-D Secure challenge and may not come back, and the provider's webhook arrives late, out of order or twice, so an order created on the thank-you page can be lost and one created per request without a key can be duplicated. Checkout carries every order at peak load and its payment page falls under the card industry's script rules, so code the platform cannot limit in time or isolate puts every order at risk; and the platform ships its own checkout changes (new payment methods, compliance fixes) into its template, so a merchant's edited copy misses them. Webhooks can also stop arriving, so a daily job asks the provider about every order still pending.

supporting_claims.claim: A cart is a draft that reserves and promises nothing, checkout is a short, clocked sequence that asks for final answers, and the order is the record every later system must keep, so whatever checkout writes into the order every later system inherits.

Checkout owns none of the facts it writes: each answer comes from the system that owns it and must be fresh enough at the moment of commitment, so a stale answer (the Phantom Stock) is fixed in the system that answers the call, not in checkout.

Because the shopper leaves for her bank or a 3-D Secure challenge and the payment provider reports by webhook, late, out of order, twice or never, the order is created once, keyed on the cart and the payment, the provider's signed message marks it paid, and a daily job asks the provider about every order still pending.
Guest checkout, express wallets, abandoned-cart recovery and business buyers change which steps the shopper sees and when the calls are made, not the calls themselves.

The four ways to run checkout trade the merchant's freedom to change it against the orchestration, card-security and upgrade work the merchant takes on, so most merchants should take the most restricted option that still gives them the two or three changes they need through sanctioned extension points.

Platforms restrict merchant code in checkout to named extension points with time limits, on dated deadlines, because merchant code there can delay order creation at peak, a script on the payment page can read card numbers, and an edited template cannot follow the platform's upgrades; the merchant's defence is an inventory of each customization with its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

role.contribution: Shows the moment the catalog's answers become an order and introduces the two mechanisms the rest of the part relies on: the payment provider's message as the only source of the payment's outcome, and the key that makes a repeated request harmless.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to wrong: three requests, then the calls, rules, worked example and variants that answer Daniel's and Sanne's
abandoned to stages: Milan's requests; four options on the same criteria, the dated case, the fit by stage, then the rule they support

flow.rationale: The three requests come first so every term arrives as part of an answer. Cart, checkout and order are defined before the calls because the calls fill the order. The calls come before the clocks because the clocks limit how long the orchestration may hold its state, and the detour in the payment step is where the two rules come from. Eva's checkout follows the clocks directly because it puts every call and both rules on one order and answers Daniel's request; guest checkout, wallets and business buyers come after it because each changes the steps of a checkout the reader has just seen whole. The failures follow because each is a broken call or rule already seen working, whoever the buyer. The last four sections answer Milan's requests: abandoned carts first, because they use the shopper's clock, the calls made on the cart and the degradation ladder from the failures; then the four ways to run checkout, then Shopify's dated withdrawal as the evidence; then the stage table, which uses the options and the warning signs from the failures and places Kestrel & Pine, and ends with the author's rule drawn from all three. Evidence comes before the rule because no section declares assertion-evidence for it. Putting the options before the failures (the published order) split the orchestration half in two; putting Eva's checkout before the calls would show answers without their owners.

hook.content: While a shopper checks out, a price can change, another customer can buy the last item and the payment response can arrive late; a successful-looking purchase can still leave the customer with unavailable goods, an unexpected total or a second order after a retry.

bridge.from_reader_world: Every reader has clicked 'pay' and seen a thank-you page, and assumes the order then exists and is paid.
bridge.to_topic: Behind that page several systems each supply one answer, and the shopper may leave for her bank's app and never come back; the question is how those answers become one order, created once, and why platforms limit what merchants may change there.

thesis_statement.text: Checkout asks the owner of each fact (price, tax, availability, delivery promise, payment state) for a final answer, creates the order once however often a request is repeated, and leaves the payment provider's message to mark it paid; because every order passes through it, platforms limit where merchants may add their own code.

sections.heading: The Cart Is a Draft, the Checkout Is a Commitment
sections.controlling_idea: A cart is a draft that reserves and promises nothing, checkout is the short, clocked sequence that asks for final answers, and the order is the record every later system keeps, so a stale answer written at checkout becomes everyone's error.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the three terms the rest of the chapter depends on and states why what checkout writes matters.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Answering Noor's question starts with three words that are easy to blur: cart, checkout and order.

A cart is a draft the shopper can still change: it reserves no stock and promises no price, and whether to reserve stock when an item is added is the first business decision about checkout, which most platforms answer no.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A checkout is the short, clocked sequence that turns the cart into an order and is the first moment the platform asks every other capability for a final answer rather than an estimate.

transition_in.introduces: The second word, checkout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An order is the record that exists when checkout succeeds, which belongs to order management from that moment, and the three differ in lifetime, who may change them, stock, price and owner.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The distinction matters because every later system treats the order as a promise, so a stale price or stock figure written into it becomes the error of the warehouse, finance and the customer.

sections.heading: What Checkout Must Call
sections.controlling_idea: Each checkout step calls a system that owns a fact, checkout owns none of them, and each answer has its own freshness need, so checkout is an orchestration, a coordinator and not an owner.

advances_thesis.how: Lists the calls, states that checkout owns none of the facts and gives each call's freshness, which is where a stale answer enters.

flow.rationale: The step table first, then what it shows (no owned facts, different freshness), then the name for that shape.

transition_in.carries_over: The order as a promise every later system inherits.
transition_in.introduces: What checkout calls to fill that promise.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each checkout step is a call to a system that owns a fact, and each makes a promise to the shopper.

evidence.what: Six steps (identity, address, shipping options, price review, payment, confirmation) with what each calls and the promise it makes.
evidence.shows: The reader can draw a checkout's call sequence from it.

evidence.what: Baymard 2024: 5.1 steps and 11.3 form fields on average; eight fields suffice.
evidence.shows: Shows that the steps vary by vendor while the calls stay the same.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout owns none of the facts it writes: price, tax, stock, delivery promise and payment state each live in another system, and tax, for example, is computed from three facts the shop holds (the ship-to address, the product's tax category and whether the buyer is a business).

transition_in.carries_over: The calls in the step table.
transition_in.introduces: What they reveal: checkout only consumes the facts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The calls also differ in how fresh their answer must be: a description may be hours old, a price minutes, and availability must be current at the moment of commitment or the order is a Phantom Stock waiting to happen.

evidence.what: Price and promotions, tax, availability, shipping and payment against freshness, consistency, illustrative latency targets and behaviour when down.
evidence.shows: Shows which answers may come from a copy and which may not, and that payment and order creation are never guessed.

transition_in.carries_over: Checkout owns none of the facts.
transition_in.introduces: The second thing the calls reveal: each answer has its own freshness need, and what to do when a call is down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: That is why checkout is called an orchestration: a coordinator that calls several services in sequence, holds a short-lived state and completes or abandons the whole.

evidence.what: Figure 3: checkout asks six systems for a final answer and creates the order once.
evidence.shows: Shows the orchestration and that it owns none of the facts.

sections.heading: The Clock and the Detour
sections.controlling_idea: Checkout runs against the shopper's patience and the payment provider's session, and inside the payment step the shopper leaves for her bank, so the order must be created once, keyed on the cart and the payment, and the provider's message must decide that it is paid.

advances_thesis.how: Derives the two rules (one order despite retries; the payment outcome as external truth) from the clocks and the detour.

flow.rationale: The two clocks and the detour are the problem; the two rules are the answer, each followed by its evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: Checkout as an orchestration with a short-lived state.
transition_in.introduces: The clocks that limit how long that state may live, and the detour where checkout loses sight of the shopper.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout runs against two clocks it does not control.
The first clock is the shopper's patience, and three of the five leading reasons for abandonment are architecture: showing total cost early, a credible delivery date and not forcing an account.

evidence.what: Baymard 2026: extra costs 40%, delivery too slow 20%, card trust 19%, forced account 18%, too long 17% (multi-select, US adults who abandoned).
evidence.shows: Ties each architectural call (tax and shipping on the cart, the delivery promise, a customer reference) to a stated reason for leaving.

transition_in.introduces: The first, the shopper's patience.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second clock is the payment provider's: a payment session expires in minutes to days by method, so checkout must finish inside the session while capturing the money can wait.

evidence.what: Mollie: iDEAL 15 minutes, cards 30 minutes, PayPal 6 hours, Klarna 48 hours; wait for the webhook. Stripe and Adyen: card authorizations valid 5 to 7 days.
evidence.shows: Gives the deadlines checkout works inside.
evidence.source: Mollie, Stripe, Adyen documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.introduces: The second clock, the payment provider's.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Inside the payment step the shopper leaves for her bank's app or a 3-D Secure challenge and may never return, and the platform learns the outcome only from webhooks that arrive late, out of order and sometimes twice, from which two rules follow.

evidence.what: Stripe: 'You can't rely on triggering fulfillment only from your checkout landing page, because it's not guaranteed customers visit that page.'
evidence.shows: Shows that the thank-you page cannot be the trigger.

transition_in.introduces: What happens inside it: the detour and the webhook.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first rule: create the order once despite retries, with an idempotency key derived from the cart and the payment rather than from each page load.

transition_in.introduces: The first rule and the idempotency key.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vendors document the key on order creation: Stripe requires fulfilment to tolerate repeated calls for the same checkout session, and commercetools creates the order once with the payment pending so that later notifications update it rather than create another.

evidence.what: commercetools checkout payments lifecycle; Stripe fulfilment guide.
evidence.shows: Shows the pattern is documented practice that tells a new purchase from another attempt at the same one.
evidence.source: commercetools and Stripe documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The idempotency key on order creation.
transition_in.introduces: Two vendors that build checkout this way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second rule: treat the payment outcome as external truth, decided by the provider's signed webhook, with a daily job asking the provider about every order still pending because webhooks stop retrying.

evidence.what: Mollie stops after ten attempts over 26 hours, Stripe after three days.
evidence.shows: Shows why a scheduled check must back up the webhook.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the order exists before the payment outcome is known; the webhook moves it to paid or failed and a repeat changes nothing.
evidence.shows: Shows the two rules working together.

transition_in.introduces: The second rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An express wallet reuses the shopper's saved payment and address details, so she confirms instead of typing, and gives the merchant a payment token in place of the card details.

transition_in.introduces: A second way: the express wallet.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Wallets shorten the visible steps (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Shop Pay's 32% of Shopify's Black Friday weekend orders), but pricing, tax, availability and shipping are still called, now from inside the wallet's callback.

evidence.shows: Shows how far wallets shorten checkout and that the orchestration remains.

transition_in.introduces: Three wallets and what they leave in place.

sections.heading: What Changes When the Buyer Is a Company
sections.controlling_idea: A business buyer changes four steps and removes one: a company account, contract prices excluding VAT, a VAT number that can switch the tax treatment, payment terms instead of a payment, and a credit check against the ERP.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the largest variant: the same orchestration with different owners for identity, price, tax and payment.

flow.rationale: The steps that change, the step that disappears, the call that is added, then the example.

transition_in.carries_over: Two variants of the consumer checkout: guest checkout and express wallets.
transition_in.introduces: The buyer that changes the most steps: a company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A business customer changes three steps, removes one and adds one call; the three are the identity, price and address steps: a company account with roles and approvers, a contract price list shown excluding VAT, and a VAT identification number that can switch the tax treatment to reverse charge.
The payment step often disappears into payment terms, a receivable in the ERP rather than a PSP event, so the merchant must decide which system owns the terms and the credit limit.

evidence.what: Shopify Admin API 2026-10 payment-term types; Microsoft's Business Central–Shopify connector guidance (14 October 2026) on owning terms and credit limits.
evidence.shows: Shows that platforms model terms and that ownership must be decided.

transition_in.introduces: The step that often disappears: payment.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A credit check against the ERP is the one call a consumer checkout never makes.

transition_in.carries_over: Payment terms as a receivable in the ERP.
transition_in.introduces: The extra call that terms require.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's B2B portal runs on the shop platform's company accounts, price lists and net terms and takes 62% of wholesale orders.

evidence.what: 62% of wholesale orders arrive through the B2B portal.
evidence.shows: Grounds the section in the running example.

transition_in.carries_over: The four changes and the extra call.
transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's own business checkout.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Checkout failures fall into five kinds (duplicate order, lost outcome, stale answer, slow or failed dependency, attack), each with its own detection, recovery and prevention.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the two rules and the freshness table into detection and recovery, and answers Sanne's question about the card-testing night.

flow.rationale: Five kinds, in the order of the two rules (duplicates, lost outcomes), the freshness table (stale answers, slow dependencies) and then the attack.

transition_in.carries_over: The variants, which change the steps a buyer sees but not the calls.
transition_in.introduces: The ways those calls fail, whoever the buyer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whoever the buyer, the calls fail in the same ways, and checkout failures cluster into five kinds.
A duplicate order comes from a double click, a retry or a repeated webhook and is prevented by the idempotency key and a handler that records every event id.

transition_in.introduces: The first, the duplicate order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A lost outcome leaves the order pending while the money sits authorized, and is found and settled by a daily query to the provider, which with the two rules answers Sanne's first request: an order the provider has not confirmed stays pending and is not fulfilled.

evidence.what: Mollie's fetch-the-status pattern and id-only webhook.
evidence.shows: Shows the documented recovery and why a forged call cannot mark anything paid.

transition_in.introduces: The second, the lost outcome.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A stale answer for stock, price or tax comes from a copy that was behind, and is prevented by a current call at commitment.

evidence.what: Most of Kestrel & Pine's €96,000 Black Friday cost.
evidence.shows: Shows the cost of the stale stock answer.

transition_in.introduces: The third, the stale answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A slow or failed dependency is met with a degradation ladder decided in advance, on which payment and order creation never appear.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth, the slow or failed dependency.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An attack such as the Card-Testing Night is met with rate limits, velocity rules, a CAPTCHA on guest checkout and a kill switch for guest card payments that needs no deploy, which answers Sanne's question about the card-testing fees.

evidence.what: 48,000 bot attempts, €2,900 in fees, a 40-minute account pause.
evidence.shows: Grounds the attack in the running example.

evidence.what: Stripe on card testing; Visa's May 2025 monitoring fact sheet.
evidence.shows: Shows the documented symptoms and controls.

transition_in.introduces: The fifth, the attack, which answers Sanne's question about the card-testing fees.

sections.heading: Abandoned Carts and the Business Metric
sections.controlling_idea: Conversion is checkout's one business metric, and the architecture decides both whether an abandoned cart can be recovered and whether fewer carts are abandoned.

advances_thesis.how: Ties conversion to calls made early (tax, shipping, delivery promise) and to a cart persisted with an identity.

flow.rationale: The metric and how far its figures can be trusted first, then what the architecture can do about it.

transition_in.carries_over: Milan's requests from the opening, the ones still open after the failures.
transition_in.introduces: His first request, fewer abandoned carts, and the business measure behind it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout's one business metric is conversion, and the abandonment rate behind it is a direction, not a benchmark, because studies define cart and abandonment differently.

evidence.what: Baymard: 70.22% average across fifty studies, 2006 to 2025, range 55% to 84%; its 35% uplift claim is its own estimate.
evidence.shows: Shows the size of the problem and how far the figures can be trusted.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Recovering an abandoned cart needs a cart stored on the server and tied to an identity the merchant may contact.

evidence.what: Two preconditions for recovery: a server-side cart and a consented identity.
evidence.shows: Shows that recovery is decided by storage and consent, not by the reminder e-mail.

transition_in.introduces: What it takes to win an abandoned cart back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Preventing abandonment needs nothing new: the early total and credible date the shopper's clock (p19) asks for, and a payment step no slow internal call can fail; one sentence, so the three fixes p19 gives are not repeated.

evidence.what: A pointer back to p19's architectural fixes and to the slow-dependency failure.
evidence.shows: Answers Milan's request for fewer abandoned carts without repeating the evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: Recovering carts after they are abandoned.
transition_in.introduces: Preventing abandonment, by pointing back to the levers already shown.

sections.heading: The Choices: Four Ways to Run a Checkout
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant can run the hosted checkout as is, add sanctioned extensions, build a custom checkout on the platform's APIs or run its own checkout service, and each step away from the first adds orchestration, card-security and upgrade work.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the four options side by side on the same criteria; the author's rule follows Shopify's lessons and the stage table.

flow.rationale: Four options in order of increasing merchant responsibility, compared on the same criteria in one table. The rule they lead to comes at the end of the stage section, after Shopify's timeline and the stage table, its evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: What the architecture can do for conversion, Milan's first request.
transition_in.introduces: His second: changes to checkout itself, and who runs and may change it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Milan's delivery date and gift wrap raise who runs the checkout and who may change it, which is the merchant's choice among four options that map closely to the scale stages.
The hosted checkout as is gives the smallest card-security scope and nothing to build or break.

transition_in.introduces: The first, the hosted checkout as is, and PCI DSS scope.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The hosted checkout with sanctioned extensions lets apps add blocks and run logic at named places with fixed inputs, outputs and a time budget, so the merchant gets its changes without owning the page.

evidence.what: Shopify checkout extensibility; commercetools API Extensions with a two-second default timeout.
evidence.shows: Shows two documented forms of the extension point.

transition_in.introduces: The second, extensions at named places.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A custom or headless checkout on the platform's APIs gives full control and full responsibility for the orchestration, the payment-page scripts and API versions.

transition_in.introduces: The third, a custom checkout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An own checkout service over separate capabilities fits when one checkout must serve several storefronts, an app, a point of sale and a B2B portal, and it costs a team.

evidence.what: The four options against who runs the orchestration, customization, PCI DSS scope, upgrade risk, team needed and the stages they fit.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader place their own checkout and see what each step away from the first costs.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth, an own service, and the four compared.

sections.heading: How Protected Checkout Is: Shopify's Timeline, 2023–2026
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify's withdrawal of editable checkout templates and scripts on dated deadlines from 2023 to 2026 shows why platforms restrict merchant code in checkout: time budgets, the card industry's payment-page rules, and extension points that are withdrawn on announced dates.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated case and draws the three lessons that answer the agency's script proposal.

flow.rationale: The dates in order, then the three lessons the dates teach.

transition_in.carries_over: Option 2, which gives the merchant only what the platform allows.
transition_in.introduces: How a hosted platform decides and moves that boundary, shown by the clearest dated record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Option 2 gives the merchant only what the platform allows: a hosted platform decides where merchants put checkout code, which gives the vendor more control over upgrades and payment-page behaviour and limits what an agency can change, and Shopify's dated changes are the clearest public record of that boundary moving.
In February 2023 Shopify announced that checkout.liquid would stop working for the in-checkout pages on 13 August 2024, replaced by checkout extensibility.

evidence.what: Shopify changelog, 13 February 2023.
evidence.shows: Dates the first withdrawal and names the replacement.

transition_in.carries_over: Shopify's record as a sequence of dates.
transition_in.introduces: The first date.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The thank-you and order-status pages followed in 2025 and 2026, and Shopify Scripts were retired on 30 June 2026.

evidence.what: Shopify developer documentation and help center: 28 August 2025 (Plus), 26 August 2026 (non-Plus), Scripts 30 June 2026.
evidence.shows: Completes the dated sequence.

transition_in.introduces: The later dates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As of November 2026 advanced checkout customization is limited to Shopify Plus and to UI extensions, Shopify Functions with an instruction limit, web pixels and a branding API.

evidence.what: Shopify Functions API 2026-10: 11 million instructions per run for carts up to 200 lines.
evidence.shows: Shows the hard limits of the sanctioned mechanisms.

evidence.what: INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout: the arc is consistent with a platform that wants one checkout it can change under every merchant, keep inside card rules and keep fast at peak.
evidence.shows: Labels the author's reading of Shopify's reasons as inference.

transition_in.introduces: What remains in November 2026.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The timeline teaches three things that apply to any platform.

transition_in.introduces: Its lessons for any platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A time budget is how a platform protects checkout from the merchant's own code.

transition_in.introduces: The first, time budgets.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The payment page is where the card industry looks: PCI DSS v4.0.1 requires an inventory of payment-page scripts and tamper detection, and the agency's gift-wrap script is exactly what that rule exists for.

evidence.what: PCI DSS 6.4.3 and 11.6.1, effective 31 March 2025, PCI SSC blog of 30 January 2025.
evidence.shows: Ties the agency's script to a dated rule.

transition_in.introduces: The second, the payment page.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform will withdraw an extension point and announce the date, so the merchant keeps an inventory of every checkout customization, its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

transition_in.introduces: The third, withdrawal on a date, and the remedy.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The stage table maps the four options, what becomes necessary and the warning signs (several of them the failures above) to the scale stages, and Kestrel & Pine, a stage-3 merchant on a stage-2 checkout, keeps its checkout and changes what it calls.

transition_in.carries_over: The options, Shopify's lessons and the author's rule.
transition_in.introduces: The same advice laid out by scale stage in a table, with Kestrel & Pine's place in it and the answer to Milan's two requests.

evidence.what: Four stages against what is typical, what becomes necessary and the warning signs.
evidence.shows: The reader can find their own stage and read off the next step and the signs it is due.

evidence.what: W4 stay and surround; W1 availability service from Q4 2027; W2 OMS from 13 October 2027.
evidence.shows: Shows the remedy is in what checkout calls, not in replacing it.

evidence.what: Two extensions added in 2027: a delivery-date block and a gift-wrap option.
evidence.shows: Closes Milan's requests with the sanctioned mechanism.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rule, drawn from the four options, Shopify's three lessons and the fit by stage: take the most restricted option that still gives the two or three changes the business needs, through sanctioned extension points, because every freedom taken is a page kept working at peak, under card rules and through every release.

transition_in.carries_over: The options, Shopify's lessons and the stage table with Kestrel & Pine's place in it.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The two halves of the chapter are one argument: checkout matters because every later system inherits what it writes into the order, and that is also why platforms limit merchant code there; the page that must create each order exactly once from fresh answers at peak is the page a slow extension or a skimming script would break. So the merchant's decision is not which page to edit but which owner answers each call and which sanctioned mechanism carries each change.
conclusion.so_what: A reader can draw their checkout's call sequence, mark the answers that come from copies, check that the order is keyed on the cart and the payment and settled by webhook and a daily job, and judge an agency's proposal by its mechanism and the vendor's support date, before buying anything.

callback.to: The introduction's shopper during whose checkout a price changes, the last item sells and the payment answer arrives late.
callback.how: The first conclusion paragraph says what keeps each of those three from breaking the order.

takeaway.content: List what your checkout calls and which answers come from copies; key order creation on the cart and the payment and settle it by webhook and a daily job; inventory every checkout customization with its mechanism and the vendor's support date; take the nine questions to your own company.

hand_off.carries_over: The order created with its payment pending, and the payment provider's webhook as the only source of the payment's outcome.
hand_off.introduces: The money's own life after checkout: the four stages, the methods that change them, and refunds and chargebacks as payments flowing back.

transition_in.carries_over: Kestrel & Pine's checkout kept, with what it calls changed.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter's answer set against its opening, then what holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A price change, a sold-out item and a late payment answer break the order only when checkout writes a stale answer or trusts a page load; asked at commitment, keyed on the cart and the payment and settled by the provider's message, they do not, and the same need, a checkout that creates every order once at peak, is why platforms keep merchant code to sanctioned, time-limited places; Noor's three requests get the same answer, Daniel's and Sanne's in who answers each call and how the order is created, Milan's in sanctioned extensions.

evidence.what: The opening's three changes during checkout set against the two rules and the platform's limits.
evidence.shows: The reader can now say what keeps each change from breaking the order and why the restriction serves the same goal.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: cart, checkout and order differ in lifetime, owner and rules; the payment outcome arrives by webhook and the order is created once and settled by webhook or a reconciliation job; platforms protect checkout with time-boxed extension points (Shopify 2023 to 2026); surprise costs and slow delivery lead the reasons for abandonment, and calling tax, shipping and the delivery promise on the cart answers both.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: The points it rests on, starting with what is established.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: hosted with or without extensions fits most merchants and a custom checkout needs shared channels and a team; guest checkout is right for consumers while for business customers the account is the checkout; order-before-outcome is the robust pattern where redirects dominate.

transition_in.introduces: What changes with the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: treat checkout as a conductor that owns no fact, and keep an inventory of every checkout customization with its mechanism and the vendor's support date.

transition_in.carries_over: What is established and what depends on context.
transition_in.introduces: The author's own judgement, labelled as such.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Nine questions let the reader find, in their own company, what checkout calls and which answers are copies, how old availability can be, what settles an unreturned payment or a repeated webhook, which customizations and payment-page scripts run and when their support ends, whether tax and shipping show on the cart, what can be switched off without a deploy, and who answers for business customers.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that apply them to the reader's own company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout hands the order to two systems at once, the order record to order management and the payment request to the payment provider, and the next chapter follows the money through its own stages.

transition_in.carries_over: The questions about the reader's own checkout.
transition_in.introduces: The handoff of the order with its payment pending to the next chapter.

decision_log.decision: In this chapter Kestrel & Pine's hosted product is 'the shop platform' where the text means that product; 'platform' alone is kept where it means any vendor's platform (Shopify, commercetools).

Used Shopify's checkout.liquid timeline rather than a survey of several vendors' extension models, because it is the only publicly dated sequence that shows a platform withdrawing checkout freedom step by step; other vendors appear only where their documentation states a mechanism (commercetools' two-second timeout).

Chose 'create the order before the PSP's final answer, settle by webhook' as the recommended pattern, citing commercetools and Stripe, rather than presenting it as one option among equals, because iDEAL, Bancontact and 3-D Secure redirects make the asynchronous outcome the normal case for a European merchant; the take-aways say when the alternative is acceptable.
Kept the four checkout options at the level of 'who runs the orchestration' rather than listing vendor products, to stay platform-neutral and to map the options onto the scale stages.
Treated B2B checkout in one section with four differences and a hand-off, rather than a parallel walkthrough of Bergzicht's order, which belongs to journey-wholesale-order.
